Prohibitionist Editorial Page Of The Tennessean
Typical Of Defectors Now Supporting Medical Marijuana:
"The federal government shouldn’t hamper states that want to allow pot by prescription
for chronically ill patients. Any other course is cruel."

As is often the case, The Tennessean still seems to be heavily into reefer madness, and yet they support medical marijuana. The fact that this edit is so bad is what makes it so "good."

This demonstrates the degree to which the prohibitionists have lost the medical marijuana debate even among the hard core constituency for marijuana prohibition.

However one may qualify this support, it completely destroys the absolutist position of the Drug Czar and the hard core reefer-madness crowd. No longer are the editors dismissing medical marijuana as just some sort of dark plot by the evil "legalizers."
See

In short, the prohibitionists have lost the support of their allies in the media on a key point. Also in many parts of the country where agriculture is key, they have simultaneously lost the editorial pages on the cultivation of hemp.

The continued intransigence of the Drug Czar and the DEA on these issues will further undermine their credibility.)

POT CAN EASE PAIN OF CHRONIC PATIENTS
March 24, 1999
From The Tennessean
Editorials

WOULD you want your teen-age daughter to smoke marijuana? No. There is far too much evidence that indicates marijuana can lead to serious, dangerous addictions.

(Marijuananews note: They seem to have missed one of the major points of the IOM report.)

See
The Wall Street Journal Responds To The IOM Report
By Having Califano Defend The "Gateway Theory"

But if your daughter had cancer or AIDS, would you want her to have legal access to marijuana if it helped ease the pain and weight loss? Most parents wouldn’t hesitate before answering yes.

The debate over the medicinal use of marijuana geared up last week with the release of a report commissioned by the federal government indicating that the active components in marijuana, cannabinoids, can ease the nausea and pain experienced by some AIDS and cancer patients.

Whether pot should be prescribed to seriously ill people is not a new topic. Six states have passed initiatives legalizing the medicinal use of marijuana. Late last year in response to those initiatives, Congress passed a resolution condemning pot’s medicinal use.

Because of the federal prohibitions against marijuana, doctors are reluctant to prescribe it, even in the six states where such treatment is legal.

(Marijuananews note: They are not just "reluctant." They cannot prescribe it. That would be a violation of federal law. Also there is no place in which a "prescription" could be filled. This statement reflects their ignorance of the subject, which clearly influences their views.)

But the problem with this particular topic is that it is too often painted in extreme terms. Some of the groups pushing for "pot by prescription" also support legalized marijuana. Some anti-drug groups fear that allowing marijuana even under controlled medical supervision would send the message that pot is beneficial.

This study cuts through the hyperbole. It didn’t recommend that marijuana be sold over the counter like aspirin or dispensed freely at doctors’ offices.

Instead, the study recommends that marijuana be available for short periods of time under strict doctors’ supervision for chronic patients who can find no other relief from nausea and extreme pain.

But the study also warns that marijuana smoke is more toxic than tobacco smoke, and can damage the lungs and cause pregnant women to give birth to low birth-weight babies. The report therefore recommends the development of smokeless products such as capsules and inhalers that can deliver the beneficial components without the smoke.

There is now just one cannabinoid-based drug on the market. Patients complain that it is more expensive than marijuana and its relief is slower than smoke.

Most politicians, including President Clinton, don’t want to support the use of marijuana by prescription out of fear that they will be labeled soft on drugs. Their best bet is to support the speedy development of alternative medicines that deliver the benefits without the smoke or the stigma of marijuana.

But until those alternative drugs are developed, the federal government shouldn’t hamper states that want to allow pot by prescription for chronically ill patients. Any other course is cruel.
